stature.source: typical: the drafter's middle for browsed valley-bottom stands, inside FEIS's usual 3-6 m (about 2.5 m at ten years); tall: FEIS and Wikipedia, to about 6 m on well-drained ground; no record height was read; read 2026-11-10

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-10), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a broadly rounded clump of many erect stems from one root crown, about as wide as tall, leafy nearly to the ground, the clumps merging into continuous willow thickets on the valley floor; shiny green in summer, yellow in fall, reddish-brown twigs in winter

description: A many-stemmed willow 2-6 m tall that grows as broad, rounded clumps from a single root crown, the clumps running together into thickets on wet valley floors. Its leaves are lance-shaped to oval, up to about 10 cm, shiny above and shaggy-white when they first open. It is a willow of the mountain bottomlands of the northern Rockies, where it lines the Lamar River and Slough Creek in Yellowstone and fills the willow flats of Jackson Hole, about 1800-2400 m in Wyoming.

season_notes.winter: Bare reddish-brown stems standing out of the snow along the river; elk browse the twig tips and the flower buds.
season_notes.spring: Small upright catkins open in May and June with or just before the new leaves, which unfold silky white.
season_notes.summer: Dense shiny green thickets; the fluffy seed is shed in late July and early August onto the wet bars.
season_notes.fall: Leaves turn yellow and drop by October; beavers cut stems for their winter food piles.

riparian.water: Needs a water table near the surface all summer: stream and river banks, overflow channels, seeps, wet meadows and the beaver-pond margins of the valley floor, on moist sand and gravel; it starts from seed on fresh alluvium in full sun and suffers where water stands over its root crown for long.

range.where: the willow thickets of the valley bottoms on Yellowstone's northern range (the lower Lamar River and Slough Creek) and the willow flats and stream bottoms of Jackson Hole; the mountains of Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, Colorado and Utah to eastern Oregon and northeastern California

notes: Sandbar willow (the template) is the library's willow shrub, but it is a narrow-leaved thicket of thin, straight wands 2-4.5 m from spreading roots, on scoured bars. The card makes Booth's willow a broadly rounded, many-stemmed clump from a root crown (FEIS: a multibranched, rounded shrub, usually 3-6 m, broadly rounded with many stems on well-drained ground, dwarfed with few stems in bogs), wider (crown_width_ratio 1.0 against 0.8) and with broader leaves (Wikipedia: lance-shaped to oval, up to about 10 cm, shiny above, shaggy white hairs when young), so leaf_size_m 0.06 for an average leaf. It resprouts from the root crown and stem base after browsing or fire and forms clonal colonies (FEIS, Wikipedia); stems die back after 15-20 years (FEIS), which the template's old age class should show as dead stems in the clump. Catkins (FEIS: erect, 1-1.5 cm; Wikipedia: to 4 cm male, 7 cm female) open May-June before or with the leaves and are not drawn, as in the template. Seeds disperse late July-early August (FEIS). Habitat: riparian and lake-edge ground with a high water table, wet meadows, fens, streambanks and overflow channels, a pioneer on fresh alluvium, shade-intolerant (FEIS); hence the high floor, low shade and perennial permanence. Elevation: Wyoming about 1800-2380 m, Utah 1615-3140 m (FEIS). Lamar River and Slough Creek willows: the NPS Yellowstone beaver page (willows the beavers' preferred winter food; a recovery on the northern range since the late 1990s); the Jackson Hole willow flats are from the brief, the NPS Grand Teton plants pages say only that willows line its rivers and wetlands. Eaters: FEIS names elk (rated good in Wyoming and Montana), moose (heavy use in Wyoming, Montana and Idaho), mule and white-tailed deer (fair), beaver, small mammals, songbirds and waterfowl; palatability rises through the season and winter browsing strips the flower buds. Moose, beaver and the willow songbirds (and white-tailed deer) are not in the animal library; the mallard stands in for the waterfowl and the deer mouse for small mammals. The NPS Grand Teton trees page says willows feed and shelter moose and sandhill cranes, neither in the library. The winter twig colour (reddish-brown) is the drafter's judgement. Colours, crown profile, porosity, stems, leaf-on months and shades_water are the drafter's judgement, not from a source.
